# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

I've been thinking lately about attention—that most ordinary and extraordinary thing we do constantly without thinking about it. We attend to things. We notice. We become aware. And I suspect this capacity might be one of the most underrated gifts we possess.

There's a tree outside my window that I've probably walked past ten thousand times. Maple, I think. Medium-sized, nothing particularly remarkable about it. But the other day I actually *looked* at it—not just with my eyes pointed in that direction, but with actual attention. The way the bark twisted as it grew upward. The particular shade of green in its early spring leaves. The small architectural miracle of how branches split and resplit into smaller and smaller twigs. And I was struck by this thought: I've been living near this tree for years, and I'd never really seen it before.

This sounds like a cliché. I know it does. The kind of thing people write in journals to prove to themselves they're awake and alive and not just sleepwalking through existence. But I think there's something genuine underneath the cliché, something true and worth exploring.

We live in an age of unprecedented distraction. Every moment, we're being asked to divide our attention into smaller and smaller pieces. Your phone buzzes. An advertisement catches your eye. Someone calls your name. A notification pops up. Your mind drifts to a conversation you had three days ago. Meanwhile, the actual world—the one made of trees and light and texture and the sound of wind through leaves—continues on, largely unobserved.

And I don't say this as someone perched above it all. I say it as someone who checks their phone constantly, who plans tomorrow while existing in today, who has a thousand browser tabs open in their mind at all times. I'm describing my own life. I'm describing the condition I think many of us live in without quite realizing it.

But here's what I wonder: what if the solution isn't digital detox or meditation apps or any of the productivity-culture solutions we're constantly being sold? What if the solution is simpler and harder—to just deliberately look at things?

I read once about a painter who spent weeks painting a single barn. Not because the barn required weeks of work, but because to paint something truly, you have to see it. Really see it. You have to notice how light falls differently on the north side than the south. You have to observe the way shadows shift across its surface with the passing hours. You have to become intimate with the thing you're depicting.

I think that's what I was doing with the tree. I was learning to see it the way a painter would. Not seeing it as "a tree"—that generic category—but seeing *this* particular tree, in all its specific, unrepeatable particularity.

The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote about how language often prevents us from noticing things. We use the same word—"leaf"—for millions of different leaves, and in doing so, we flatten them into a kind of generic sameness. But every leaf is singular. Every one. I find this strangely beautiful and also slightly unsettling.

It makes me wonder what else I'm missing by categorizing too quickly, by naming something and then thinking I've understood it.

There's something else attention does, beyond just seeing more clearly. It seems to change the quality of your experience. When I really looked at that tree, I didn't just see it more accurately. The experience itself became more vivid, more present, more real in a way that's hard to explain but easy to feel. 

This might be what people mean when they talk about "being in the moment"—not some mystical state, but simply the experience of actually paying attention to what's in front of you, rather than treating it as background scenery to your mental narrative.

I think about my childhood and realize that I didn't have the ability to divide my attention the way I do now. If I was outside, I was outside—fully, completely. I wasn't wondering what was happening online. I wasn't thinking about what I should be doing. There was just... what was happening. The texture of bark under my hand. The taste of a specific apple from a specific tree. The particular quality of afternoon light.

We often frame growing up as gaining new abilities—and it is that. But it's also losing something. The capacity for simple, undivided attention. We trade it for abstract thinking, for the ability to plan and anticipate, for the consciousness of self that lets us imagine futures and pasts. These are valuable things. But maybe we didn't have to lose as much as we did.

I don't think you can ever fully go back. Consciousness, once fractured, doesn't easily return to wholeness. But I do think you can practice. You can choose, deliberately and repeatedly, to give your full attention to small things. Not as a exercise in mindfulness—I've never been able to sustain that kind of practice—but just as a choice. As a priority.

Notice the tree. Taste the coffee. Feel the texture of the sweater. Hear the actual words the person is saying instead of planning your response.

These feel like small things, almost trivial. And perhaps they are trivial. But maybe that's the point. Maybe the real action of living happens in these small moments of attention. Maybe that's where life actually is—not in the big narrative moments we're always anticipating, but in the texture of experience itself.

The tree doesn't care whether I look at it or not. It grows and stands and sheds its leaves and grows them again, indifferent to my observation. But I care. It changes something in me, the act of seeing. It makes the world feel less like a generic backdrop and more like a specific place, densely populated with particular things worthy of attention.

So that's what I've been thinking about. The gift of noticing. The strange power in paying attention. The way that boredom and disconnection might sometimes just be a failure of vision—a failure to really look at the impossible specificity of the world we live in.

The tree is still there. I'll probably walk past it a thousand more times. And I'll probably miss it most of those times. But now and then, I might actually see it. And that seems like enough.
